name: Rhodiola rosea

lead: Rhodiola rosea is an Arctic and mountain succulent whose root is sold as an adaptogen for stress, fatigue and stamina. People use it to stay energised and recover, which supports more consistent training and a fitter, fresher appearance.

Its rosavins and salidroside are reported in cell and animal studies to have antioxidant, neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory activity. A 2010 review summarised its clinical efficacy, while a 2012 European Medicines Agency report described the published trials as having considerable quality deficiencies. Some forum posts discuss hormone effects, but no study cited tests that.

paras: It is taken as a standardised root extract in capsules, usually in the morning around work or training. Users generally report noticing effects on fatigue over days to a few weeks, and combine it with other adaptogens and sleep and recovery habits.

FDA has issued warning letters over unapproved health claims. The plant is listed under CITES Appendix II because wild populations are overharvested, and products can be adulterated. Human adverse effects are not well covered in the sources reviewed. It is sold as a supplement.

angle.text: Rhodiola is taken as an adaptogen for stress and fatigue: less fatigue means better energy and training capacity, which supports a fitter, fresher look. Human trials on fatigue vary in quality.

lead: Rhodiola rosea, known as golden root, rose root or Arctic root, is a perennial succulent in the stonecrop family (Crassulaceae) that grows in cold, high-altitude and Arctic regions of Europe, Asia and North America.[1][2] Its rhizome is used in traditional medicine and sold as an adaptogen: a supplement promoted for stress, fatigue and stamina.[1][2]

The rhizome contains roughly 140 compounds, including the phenylpropanoids rosavin, rosarin and rosin and the phenylethanoid salidroside.[1] A 2010 review summarised its traditional use, chemistry and clinical efficacy, and laboratory work on salidroside reports neuroprotective, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects in cells and animals.[2][3][4][5]

Wikipedia states that researchers have found no high-quality clinical evidence that the plant treats any disease, and cites a 2012 European Medicines Agency report that described published trials as having considerable quality deficiencies.[1] No study found in these sources tests rhodiola for appearance outcomes.
infobox: Golden root, rose root, Arctic root[1]

paras: Wikipedia reports the plant has a history in traditional medicine and is sold in Asia and Eastern Europe as capsules, liquid extracts and tablets; Pedanius Dioscorides described it in De Materia Medica and Carl Linnaeus later named it.[1] The 2010 Phytomedicine review covers its traditional use in Scandinavia, Russia and Asia, and a 1999 paper grouped it with other adaptogenic herbs in Ayurvedic and related medicine.[2][6]

Salidroside is the most studied constituent in the laboratory. Cell and animal studies report that it protects neuroblastoma cells against oxidative and amyloid-induced injury,[7][8] stimulates the Sirt1/PGC-1 alpha axis in a mouse diabetic-nephropathy model,[9] and inhibits inflammatory signalling in psoriasis-related and endothelial cell models.[4][4] Wikipedia notes that rosavin, rosarin, rosin and salidroside have no demonstrated physiological effect in humans.[1] A 2011 review of herbal medicines for depression, anxiety and insomnia discusses rhodiola among the herbs examined.[10]

The 2010 review assessed clinical studies, mainly of fatigue, stress and mood, and Wikipedia cites the EMA's 2012 conclusion that published trials showed considerable deficiencies in quality.[2][1] Registered trials include studies of Rhodiola crenulata in COPD (57) and in acute mountain sickness (125),[11][12] adults with ADHD (two Phase 4 studies of 60 each),[13][14] mental and physical fatigue (90),[15] and several small exercise and cognition studies in athletes and healthy adults (13 to 27 participants).[16][17] The sources consulted give no results for these, and none tests a cosmetic or appearance outcome.

Wikipedia states the US FDA has issued warning letters to supplement makers over unapproved health claims for rhodiola, including claims about Raynaud syndrome, altitude sickness, depression and cancer.[1] The plant is listed under CITES Appendix II, and demand has led to overharvesting of wild populations and to adulteration of products.[1] A US homeopathic-style adrenal product label lists rhodiola among its ingredients with advice to consult a professional if pregnant or breastfeeding.[18]
